title: Sequence surge heuristic simulation labbook
content:
Purpose and context:
This doc captures exploratory simulation work on sequence-surge scenarios (sudden arrival of long-context requests) and how kernel-selection heuristics + prefetch/backpressure interact with latency SLOs and throughput. Goal: produce lightweight rules-of-thumb and failure modes for the scheduler/kernelselection team and identify follow-up microbench experiments.

Background and motivation:
- We've seen a couple customer incidents where a scheduled batch job or a user-driven long-prompt causes a transient p99 spike that propagates across the node due to KV-cache thrash and kernel handoffs.
- Existing kernels: flash (flashpaged/FlashAttention-like fused ops), paged-attn (paged KV management), and fused-ops fallback stack. Heuristics pick based on seq_len, batch_size, free_mem, and recent throughput.
- Hypothesis: Short bursts of long sequences create a cascade: large KV writes -> scheduled prefetches -> higher occupancy -> delayed small-request service because the kernel scheduler prefers throughput-efficient kernels for the long requests. Also, kernel switch overheads + fusion priming cause microstutter.

Experiment design (simulation + synthetic driver):
- Two-layer approach: discrete-event simulator + synthetic workload runs on a single 80GB-GPU instance (for validation).
- Workload mix: baseline small-chat requests (seq 64, mean tokens 40, poisson arrival lambda=120qps) + injected surge of long requests (seq 4096, single-shot at t=60s, then spike lasting 10s with 8 concurrent long reqs).
- Variants: with/without KV-prefetch, with conservatively aggressive prefetch, with kernel affinity threshold tuned (flash if seq>=256 and batch>=4), with immediate kernel swap policy vs delayed swap (drain current wave).
- Metrics recorded: p50/p95/p99 latency per class, tail amplification (ratio of small-request p99 during/after surge to baseline), kernel-switch count, prefetch I/O bytes, active warp occupancy trace, and GPU utilization.

Key simulation assumptions (approx):
- Flash kernel setup cost: 0.9ms fixed priming + per-token cost 0.02ms
- Paged-attn per-token cost slightly higher (0.025ms) but negligible priming
- Kernel switch overhead: 0.6ms pipeline stall + 2ms warmup for fusedops cache (depending on opcache state)
- KV-prefetch issues: prefetch can reduce subsequent per-token cost by 20% but occupies 10% of memory bandwidth and increases peak occupancy.
- These numbers are conservative/parametric; real runs will validate.

Observations from sim runs (delta vs baseline):
1) Baseline (no surge): small-requests p99 ~ 18ms, throughput stable.
2) Immediate kernel-swap policy: surge causes small-requests p99 to spike to ~95ms (tail amplification x5) during the 10s window. Root cause: scheduler preempts GPU for long requests using flash kernel; kernel swap + priming stalls small batches queued behind.
3) Delayed-swap (allow current microbatch drain before switching): p99 spikes reduced to ~45ms, but longer tail at p95 for long requests. Trade-off: better short-request experience, worse long-request latency.
4) Aggressive prefetch enabled: further reduces long-request average latency by 12%, but increases small-request p99 by 8–12% (due to bandwidth contention).
5) Conservative prefetch (prefetch only when long-request > 2 concurrent): removes most small-request penalty while retaining ~7% long-request improvement.
6) Kernel-switch count correlates with p99: each extra switch in the window adds ~6–8ms to p99 of queued small requests (synthetic sim).

Microbench validation notes (single GPU):
- Ran the surge waveform with driver harness (see linked PR) on an A100-80GB replica. Verified qualitative patterns: immediate swap policy shows microstutter of ~50–120ms on small chats; delayed-swap reduced microstutter but increased long-request 95th.
- Observed KV-eviction waves (measured via kv-cache hits) when more than 3 long requests overlap. Evictions correlate with 12–18ms extra latency for subsequent continuation tokens.
- Warp occupancy traces (NVIDIA CUPTI + internal tracer) show 20–30% increase in occupancy during fused flash kernel but also 15–20% more SM-level memory pressure. This aligns with the bandwidth contention hypothesis.

Hypotheses and interpretation:
- Root cause path: surge -> scheduler picks throughput-optimized kernel (flash) -> priming + high occupancy -> small requests queued -> kernel swap overheads + prefetch bandwidth hurt small-request tails.
- Prefetch is a double-edged sword: helps long sequences but can make small requests worse unless gated by concurrency thresholds.
- Kernel switch hysteresis helps short-request SLOs at cost of long-request p95; there's a sweet spot where delayed swap latency cost is acceptable given SLA mix.

Quick rules-of-thumb from sim+microbench:
- If small_request_SLO_strict (p99 <= 30ms): enable delayed-swap with drain_size ~ current_coalesced_batch and conservative prefetch gating (concurrency >= 2).
- If long_request_throughput_key: prefer immediate swap + aggressive prefetch, but maintain a per-tenant concurrency cap to prevent cross-tenant tail amplification.
- Kernel swap penalty is roughly proportional to number of queued microbatches at swap time; avoid swaps when queue_depth > 4.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Multi-tenant impact: simulate cross-tenant resource isolation (dedicated CUDA streams vs shared) to see if per-tenant stream isolation reduces tail.
- More accurate quantification of prefetch bandwidth cost on different GPU models (H100 vs A100).
- Explore hybrid kernel that maintains lightweight priming to reduce swap cost (proto: keep a warmed opcache with a single flash allocation). Feasibility: memory overheads? implement prototype.
- Integrate with routing policies: consider short-request fast-path that binds to reserved low-occupancy worker pool during detected surge. Estimate cost of reserving 5-10% capacity.

Action items (owners):
- Asha: produce deterministic microbench harness that can replay the surge waveform and emit kernel-switch traces (due 2025-03-07). linked PR for harness in artifacts.
- Marcus: run multi-GPU variants and compare A100 vs H100 prefetch effect (due 2025-03-14).
- Evelyn: prototype delayed-swap heuristic in scheduler and run controlled A/B (due 2025-03-10).
- Jon: draft a short one-pager for product/CS describing SLO trade-offs and recommended tenant config defaults (due 2025-03-12).

Notes and loose thoughts:
- Observability: we need per-token kernel attribution in traces (not just per-request) so we can see which tokens paid the swap cost.
- Consider exposing a "surge-protection" flag per deployment to enable delayed-swap + reserved capacity for latency-sensitive customers.
- Could be useful to add a cheap heuristic: if incoming request sequence length > max_seen_in_last_T and queue_depth > X, route to dedicated low-occupancy worker. Simple to implement in policy layer.

Appendix: quick parameter table used in sim (for reference)
- flash_priming_ms: 0.9
- flash_per_token_ms: 0.02
- paged_per_token_ms: 0.025
- kernel_switch_fixed_ms: 0.6
- kernel_warmup_extra_ms: 2.0
- prefetch_bandwidth_frac: 0.10
- small_request_baseline_p99_ms: 18

End of labbook. Comments welcome — this is intentionally exploratory.
